source: The Yajurveda lists eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta. Wh

items.question: The Yajurveda lists eka, dasha, shata, sahasra and ayuta. Which numbers are these, and how is each one related to the one before it?
steps: eka is one and dasha is ten: 10 × 1 = 10.
shata is a hundred: 10 × 10 = 100.
sahasra is a thousand: 10 × 100 = 1000.
ayuta is ten thousand: 10 × 1000 = 10000.
Each name is 10 times the one before it, so the names follow powers of 10, just as we say numbers today.
items.answer: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before

videos.answer: 1, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000; each is 10 times the one before

source: In the morning a herder keeps one stick for each cow. In the

items.question: In the morning a herder keeps one stick for each cow. In the evening she takes out one stick for each cow that returns, and 2 sticks are left. Her neighbour's stick bundle, paired stick by stick with hers, has 3 sticks without partners. What can she say?
steps: Each returning cow removes exactly one stick, so every stick left stands for a cow that did not return.
2 sticks are left, so 2 cows are still missing.
Pairing her sticks with the neighbour's sticks one to one, the 3 unpaired sticks are on the neighbour's side.
So she has fewer cows than her neighbour, and she needs 3 more cows to have the same number.
items.answer: 2 cows are missing; she has fewer cows than her neighbour and needs 3 more

videos.answer: 2 cows are missing; she has fewer cows than her neighbour and needs 3 more

source: Using the letters a to z as a counting sequence, which lette

items.question: Using the letters a to z as a counting sequence, which letter counts the 20th object, and what happens with 27 objects? Then use Table 1 to write 13 and 18 in Roman symbols.
steps: Match the objects with a, b, c, ... in order: the 20th letter of the alphabet is t.
The alphabet has only 26 letters, so the 27th object has no letter; the sequence runs out.
In Table 1, 13 is X followed by three I's: XIII.
18 is X, then V, then three I's: XVIII.
items.answer: The 20th object is t; 27 objects cannot be counted; 13 is XIII and 18 is XVIII

videos.answer: The 20th object is t; 27 objects cannot be counted; 13 is XIII and 18 is XVIII

source: Compare the three counting methods (sticks, letters a to z,

items.question: Compare the three counting methods (sticks, letters a to z, Roman symbols) on two questions: does the sequence ever end, and is it easy to count a large collection with it?
steps: Sticks: add one more stick each time, so the sequence never ends; but 500 cows need 500 sticks, which is slow and heavy.
Letters: easy to say quickly, but after z there is no next letter, so it ends at 26.
Roman symbols: compact, but bigger and bigger numbers keep needing new symbols.
None of the three is both unending and easy; that is the challenge a good number system must meet.
items.answer: Sticks never end but are slow; letters are quick but end at 26; Roman symbols need ever new symbols

videos.answer: Sticks never end but are slow; letters are quick but end at 26; Roman symbols need ever new symbols

source: Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 1)

items.question: Suppose you are using the number system that uses sticks to represent numbers, as in Method 1. Without using either the number names or the numerals of the Hindu number system, give a method for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing two numbers or two collections of sticks.
steps: To add, put the two collections of sticks together; the joined pile is the sum.
To subtract, pair each stick of the smaller pile with a stick of the larger pile and take the pairs away; the unpaired sticks are the difference.
To multiply, lay out the first pile once for every stick of the second pile and join all the copies.
To divide, keep taking out groups the size of the second pile; the number of groups is the quotient and the sticks that cannot make a full group are the remainder.
items.answer: Add by joining, subtract by pairing and removing, multiply by repeating one pile once per stick of the other, divide by taking out equal groups

videos.answer: Add by joining, subtract by pairing and removing, multiply by repeating one pile once per stick of the other, divide by taking out equal groups

source: Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 2)

items.question: One way of extending the number system in Method 2 is by using strings with more than one letter, for example, we could use 'aa' for 27. How can you extend this system to represent all the numbers? There are many ways of doing it!
steps: After z, start again with doubled letters: aa, bb, cc, ..., zz count the next 26 objects.
Then use tripled letters aaa, bbb, ..., zzz for the next 26, and so on.
Another way: after z use aa, ab, ac, ..., az, then ba, bb, ..., like the columns of a spreadsheet.
Either way, longer strings can always be made, so the sequence never runs out.
items.answer: One way: a to z, then aa, bb, ..., zz, then aaa, bbb, ..., zzz and so on; many other ways work

videos.answer: One way: a to z, then aa, bb, ..., zz, then aaa, bbb, ..., zzz and so on; many other ways work

source: Figure it Out (the mechanism of counting, question 3)

items.question: Try making your own number system.
steps: Choose a standard sequence with a fixed order: objects, sounds or written marks.
Check that it never runs out: decide how to make the next symbol after any symbol.
Check that it is easy to count with: for example, give a new mark to every group of five.
Test it by writing a few numbers, such as the number of students in your class.
items.answer: Open answer: any fixed-order sequence that never runs out and is easy to count with

videos.answer: Open answer: any fixed-order sequence that never runs out and is easy to count with

source: The Lebombo bone has 29 notches. Group them in fives. How ma

items.question: The Lebombo bone has 29 notches. Group them in fives. How many full groups are there, and how many notches are left over?
steps: Count off five notches at a time: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
That is 5 full groups of five, and 5 × 5 = 25.
29 − 25 = 4, so 4 notches are left over.
So the 29 notches read as 5 groups of five and 4 more: 5 × 5 + 4 = 29.
items.answer: 5 groups of five and 4 more

videos.answer: 5 groups of five and 4 more

source: In the Gumulgal system, urapon is 1 and ukasar is 2. Build t

items.question: In the Gumulgal system, urapon is 1 and ukasar is 2. Build the names for 5 and 6, and say what a Gumulgal speaker would say for 7.
steps: Split 5 into twos and a one: 5 = 2 + 2 + 1.
So 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon.
6 = 2 + 2 + 2, so 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar.
Any number greater than 6 was simply called ras.
items.answer: 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and 7 is ras

videos.answer: 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar, and 7 is ras

source: In a system that counts only by 5s, how would 1345 be writte

items.question: In a system that counts only by 5s, how would 1345 be written? How many group symbols are needed?
steps: Find how many fives make 1345: 1345 ÷ 5 = 269.
Check: 269 × 5 = 1345, so nothing is left over.
So 1345 needs the symbol for five written 269 times.
That is far too many symbols to write or read, so a single group size soon becomes cumbersome.
items.answer: 269 symbols for five, too many to write or read easily

videos.answer: 269 symbols for five, too many to write or read easily

source: Figure it Out (early number systems, question 1)

items.question: A group of indigenous people in a Pacific island use different sequences of number names to count different objects. Why do you think they do this?
steps: Think about what was being counted: fish, coconuts, canoes, days.
Things that come in bunches or pairs may be easier to count in their own groups.
A separate sequence also tells the listener what kind of object is meant.
So the sequences may follow how each kind of object is usually grouped, traded or used.
items.answer: Open answer: for example, each kind of object is grouped or traded in its own way, and the name also tells what is being counted

videos.answer: Open answer: for example, each kind of object is grouped or traded in its own way, and the name also tells what is being counted

source: Figure it Out (early number systems, question 2)

items.question: Consider the extension of the Gumulgal number system beyond 6 in the same way of counting by 2s. Come up with ways of performing the different arithmetic operations (+, −, ×, ÷) for numbers occurring in this system, without using Hindu numerals. Use this to evaluate the following: (i) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) + (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) (ii) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) − (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) (iii) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) × (ukasar-ukasar) (iv) (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) ÷ (ukasar-ukasar)
steps: (i) Join the words: 4 ukasar and 3 ukasar give 7 ukasar, and the two urapons make one more ukasar, so 8 ukasar. Check: 9 + 7 = 16.
(ii) Take 3 ukasar away from 4 ukasar and an urapon: ukasar-urapon is left. Check: 9 − 6 = 3.

(iii) ukasar-ukasar is two twos, so write the first number two times and then double the result, 4 copies in all: 16 ukasar and 4 urapons, and the 4 urapons make 2 more ukasar, so 18 ukasar. Check: 9 × 4 = 36.
(iv) Share 8 ukasar into groups of ukasar-ukasar: there are 4 groups, written ukasar-ukasar. Check: 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
items.answer: (i) ukasar written 8 times (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar written 18 times (iv) ukasar-ukasar

videos.answer: (i) ukasar written 8 times (ii) ukasar-urapon (iii) ukasar written 18 times (iv) ukasar-ukasar

source: Write 2367 as a sum of Roman landmark numbers and then as a

items.question: Write 2367 as a sum of Roman landmark numbers and then as a Roman numeral.
steps: One 10 fits: 17 − 10 = 7. One 5 fits: 7 − 5 = 2, which is two 1s.
Writing one symbol for each landmark, 2367 is written as MMCCCLXVII.

source: Add CCXXXII and CCCCXIII without converting them to Hindu nu

items.question: Add CCXXXII and CCCCXIII without converting them to Hindu numerals.
steps: Count the symbols: C's 2 + 4 = 6, X's 3 + 1 = 4, I's 2 + 3 = 5.
Five I's make one V.
Four X's are written as XL, ten less than fifty.
Six C's: five C's make a D, and one C is left, so DC.
The sum is DCXLV. Check with our numerals: 232 + 413 = 645.
items.answer: DCXLV

videos.answer: DCXLV

source: Add LXXXVII and LXXVIII without converting them to Hindu num

items.question: Add LXXXVII and LXXVIII without converting them to Hindu numerals.
steps: Count the symbols: L's 1 + 1 = 2, X's 3 + 2 = 5, V's 1 + 1 = 2, I's 2 + 3 = 5.
Five I's make a V, so now there are 3 V's: two of them make an X and one V stays.
That gives 6 X's: five make an L and one X stays, so now there are 3 L's.
Two L's make a C and one L stays.
The sum is CLXV. Check with our numerals: 87 + 78 = 165.
items.answer: CLXV

videos.answer: CLXV

source: Find V × L, L × D, V × D and VII × IX in Roman numerals.

items.question: Find V × L, L × D, V × D and VII × IX in Roman numerals.
steps: V × L is 5 × 50 = 250, which is 100 + 100 + 50, written as CCL.
L × D is 50 × 500 = 25000, which is 25 thousands, written as M repeated 25 times.
V × D is 5 × 500 = 2500, which is 1000 + 1000 + 500, written as MMD.
VII × IX is 7 × 9 = 63, which is 50 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1, written as LXIII.
None of these products is a single landmark symbol, so there is no simple rule.
items.answer: V × L is CCL, L × D is 25 M's, V × D is MMD and VII × IX is LXIII

videos.answer: V × L is CCL, L × D is 25 M's, V × D is MMD and VII × IX is LXIII

source: Figure it Out (Roman numerals, question 1)

items.question: Represent the following numbers in the Roman system. (i) 1222 (ii) 2999 (iii) 302 (iv) 715
steps: (ii) 2999 = 1000 + 1000 + 900 + 90 + 9; 900 is CM, 90 is XC and 9 is IX, so it is written as MMCMXCIX.
(iii) 302 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 1 + 1, written as CCCII.
(iv) 715 = 500 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 5, written as DCCXV.
items.answer: (i) MCCXXII (ii) MMCMXCIX (iii) CCCII (iv) DCCXV

videos.answer: (i) MCCXXII (ii) MMCMXCIX (iii) CCCII (iv) DCCXV

source: Figure it Out (early number systems, question 3)

items.question: Identify the features of the Hindu number system that make it efficient when compared to the Roman number system.
steps: Place value: in our numerals the position of a digit tells its landmark, so ten digits write every number; Roman symbols have fixed values and need new symbols for bigger numbers.
Zero: we have a digit 0 for an empty place; the Roman system has no symbol for zero.
Calculation: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing follow simple column rules in our system, while Roman numerals make them very hard.
items.answer: Place value with ten digits, a symbol for zero, and easy calculation

videos.answer: Place value with ten digits, a symbol for zero, and easy calculation

Add a group size: give a new symbol to a group, such as five marks.
Add landmark numbers: give new symbols to bigger groups too, such as five groups of five.
Write a few numbers in the refined system and check that they are shorter than before.

source: Write 2153 in Egyptian numerals.

items.question: Write 2153 in Egyptian numerals.
steps: The largest landmark that fits is 1000: two of them, 2153 − 2000 = 153.
Five 10s fit: 53 − 50 = 3, which is three 1s.
It is written as 2 lotuses, 1 coil, 5 heels and 3 strokes.
items.answer: 2 lotuses, 1 coil, 5 heels and 3 strokes

videos.answer: 2 lotuses, 1 coil, 5 heels and 3 strokes

source: An Egyptian numeral shows 3 lotuses, 4 heels and 6 strokes.

items.question: An Egyptian numeral shows 3 lotuses, 4 heels and 6 strokes. What number is it?
steps: No coils, so no hundreds.

source: Figure it Out (Egyptian numerals, question 1)

items.question: Represent the following numbers in the Egyptian system: 10458, 1023, 2660, 784, 1111, 70707.
steps: 10458 = 10000 + 400 + 50 + 8: 1 finger, 4 coils, 5 heels and 8 strokes.
1023 = 1000 + 20 + 3: 1 lotus, 2 heels and 3 strokes. 2660 = 2000 + 600 + 60: 2 lotuses, 6 coils and 6 heels.
784 = 700 + 80 + 4: 7 coils, 8 heels and 4 strokes. 1111 = 1000 + 100 + 10 + 1: one lotus, one coil, one heel and one stroke.
70707 = 70000 + 700 + 7: 7 fingers, 7 coils and 7 strokes.
items.answer: 10458: 1 finger, 4 coils, 5 heels, 8 strokes; 1023: 1 lotus, 2 heels, 3 strokes; 2660: 2 lotuses, 6 coils, 6 heels; 784: 7 coils, 8 heels, 4 strokes; 1111: one of each of lotus, coil, heel, stroke; 70707: 7 fingers, 7 coils, 7 strokes

videos.answer: 10458: 1 finger, 4 coils, 5 heels, 8 strokes; 1023: 1 lotus, 2 heels, 3 strokes; 2660: 2 lotuses, 6 coils, 6 heels; 784: 7 coils, 8 heels, 4 strokes; 1111: one of each of lotus, coil, heel, stroke; 70707: 7 fingers, 7 coils, 7 strokes

source: Figure it Out (Egyptian numerals, question 2)

items.question: What numbers do these numerals stand for? (i) 2 coils, 7 heels and 6 strokes (ii) 4 lotuses, 3 coils, 2 heels and 2 strokes
steps: (i) 2 coils make 200, 7 heels make 70 and 6 strokes make 6.
(ii) 4 lotuses make 4000, 3 coils make 300, 2 heels make 20 and 2 strokes make 2.

source: Write 89 in the base-5 system with triangle 1, square 5, hex

items.question: Write 89 in the base-5 system with triangle 1, square 5, hexagon 25 and circle 125.
steps: 125 is bigger than 89, so start with 25: three 25s fit, 89 − 75 = 14.
Two 5s fit in 14: 14 − 10 = 4, which is four 1s.
It is written as 3 hexagons, 2 squares and 4 triangles.
items.answer: 3 hexagons, 2 squares and 4 triangles

videos.answer: 3 hexagons, 2 squares and 4 triangles

source: Find the first five landmark numbers of a base-3 system and

items.question: Find the first five landmark numbers of a base-3 system and write 50 as a sum of them.
steps: Start at 1 and multiply by 3: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81.
81 is bigger than 50, so start with 27: one fits, 50 − 27 = 23.
Two 9s fit in 23: 23 − 18 = 5. One 3 fits: 5 − 3 = 2, which is two 1s.

source: Figure it Out (base-n systems, question 1)

items.question: Write the following numbers in the above base-5 system using the symbols in Table 2: 15, 50, 137, 293, 651.
steps: 15 = 5 + 5 + 5: 3 squares. 50 = 25 + 25: 2 hexagons.
137 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1: 1 circle, 2 squares and 2 triangles.
293 = 125 + 125 + 25 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1: 2 circles, 1 hexagon, 3 squares and 3 triangles.
651 = 625 + 25 + 1: 1 wave, 1 hexagon and 1 triangle.
items.answer: 15: 3 squares; 50: 2 hexagons; 137: 1 circle, 2 squares, 2 triangles; 293: 2 circles, 1 hexagon, 3 squares, 3 triangles; 651: 1 wave, 1 hexagon, 1 triangle

videos.answer: 15: 3 squares; 50: 2 hexagons; 137: 1 circle, 2 squares, 2 triangles; 293: 2 circles, 1 hexagon, 3 squares, 3 triangles; 651: 1 wave, 1 hexagon, 1 triangle

source: Figure it Out (base-n systems, question 2)

items.question: Is there a number that cannot be represented in our base-5 system above? Why or why not?
steps: Every counting number can be grouped into powers of 5, using each symbol at most 4 times.
As numbers grow, we only need more landmark symbols, which can always be invented.
But 0 is the number of objects in an empty collection, and there is no symbol to draw for it.
So 0 cannot be represented.
items.answer: Yes: 0 cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it

videos.answer: Yes: 0 cannot be represented, because the system has no symbol for it

source: Figure it Out (base-n systems, question 3)

items.question: Compute the landmark numbers of a base-7 system. In general, what are the landmark numbers of a base-n system?
steps: Start at 1 and multiply by 7 each time: 1, 7, 7 × 7 = 49, 49 × 7 = 343, 343 × 7 = 2401.
In general, start at 1 and multiply by n each time.
So the landmarks of base n are 1, n, n², n³, and so on, the powers of n.
items.answer: Base 7: 1, 7, 49, 343, 2401, ...; base n: 1, n, n², n³, ..., the powers of n

videos.answer: Base 7: 1, 7, 49, 343, 2401, ...; base n: 1, n, n², n³, ..., the powers of n

source: Figure it Out (bases and their limits, question 1)

items.question: Can there be a number whose representation in Egyptian numerals has one of the symbols occurring 10 or more times? Why not?
steps: Every Egyptian landmark is 10 times the one before.
If a symbol appeared 10 times, those 10 symbols would make exactly one symbol of the next landmark.
Grouping always takes as many of the larger landmark as possible, so the 10 would be regrouped.
So no symbol is ever written 10 or more times.
items.answer: No: 10 of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped

videos.answer: No: 10 of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped

source: Figure it Out (bases and their limits, question 2)

items.question: Create your own number system of base 4, and represent numbers from 1 to 16.
steps: Landmarks of base 4: 1, 4, 16. Give them symbols, for example a dot for 1, a stick for 4 and a square for 16.
1, 2, 3 are 1, 2, 3 dots; 4 is a stick; 5, 6, 7 are a stick and 1, 2, 3 dots.
8 is 2 sticks; 9, 10, 11 add 1, 2, 3 dots; 12 is 3 sticks; 13, 14, 15 add 1, 2, 3 dots.
16 is one square, since four sticks make the next landmark.
items.answer: Landmarks 1, 4, 16; for example 7 is a stick and 3 dots, 12 is 3 sticks, 16 is one square

videos.answer: Landmarks 1, 4, 16; for example 7 is a stick and 3 dots, 12 is 3 sticks, 16 is one square

source: Add 8 heels and 7 strokes to 7 heels and 8 strokes in Egypti

items.question: Add 8 heels and 7 strokes to 7 heels and 8 strokes in Egyptian numerals.
steps: Count each kind: heels 8 + 7 = 15, strokes 7 + 8 = 15.
Ten strokes make one heel: 15 strokes become 1 heel and 5 strokes, so there are now 16 heels.
Ten heels make one coil: 16 heels become 1 coil and 6 heels.
The sum is 1 coil, 6 heels and 5 strokes, which is 165. Check: 87 + 78 = 165.
items.answer: 1 coil, 6 heels and 5 strokes, which is 165

videos.answer: 1 coil, 6 heels and 5 strokes, which is 165

source: Find 100 × 10, 1000 × 100 and 100 × 1000 in Egyptian numeral

items.question: Find 100 × 10, 1000 × 100 and 100 × 1000 in Egyptian numerals, and check 25 × 125 in base 5.
steps: 100 × 10 = 1000: a coil times a heel is a lotus.
1000 × 100 = 100000: a lotus times a coil is a tadpole.
100 × 1000 = 100000: a coil times a lotus is also a tadpole.
In base 5, a hexagon times a circle: 25 × 125 = 3125, which is the arrow, another landmark.
In each case the product is a single landmark symbol.
items.answer: A lotus, a tadpole, a tadpole, and in base 5 an arrow; each product is a landmark

videos.answer: A lotus, a tadpole, a tadpole, and in base 5 an arrow; each product is a landmark

source: Multiply 121 (1 coil, 2 heels, 1 stroke) by 10, then use the

items.question: Multiply 121 (1 coil, 2 heels, 1 stroke) by 10, then use the rule to find 522 × 10.
steps: So 121 × 10 = 1210: 1 lotus, 2 coils and 1 heel; every symbol moved up one landmark.
522 is 5 coils, 2 heels and 2 strokes; moving each up gives 5 lotuses, 2 coils and 2 heels, so 522 × 10 = 5220.
items.answer: 121 × 10 is 1210 (1 lotus, 2 coils, 1 heel) and 522 × 10 is 5220

videos.answer: 121 × 10 is 1210 (1 lotus, 2 coils, 1 heel) and 522 × 10 is 5220

source: Add 2907 and 43 on the counting board.

items.question: Add 2907 and 43 on the counting board.
steps: 2907 has 2 counters on the thousands line, 9 on the hundreds line (one above it for 5 and 4 on it), none for tens and 7 for ones; 43 has 4 tens and 3 ones.
Bring the ones together: 7 + 3 = 10 ones, which become 1 counter on the tens line.
Tens: 4 + 1 = 5, shown by one counter above the tens line.
Hundreds stay 9 and thousands stay 2, so the board shows 2950.

source: Figure it Out (adding with landmarks, question 1)

items.question: Add the following Egyptian numerals: (i) 9 lotuses, 6 coils and 8 strokes + 5 coils and 7 strokes (ii) 1 lotus and 8 heels + 4 heels and 6 strokes
steps: (i) Strokes 8 + 7 = 15: 1 heel and 5 strokes. Coils 6 + 5 = 11: 1 lotus and 1 coil.
Lotuses 9 + 1 = 10: 1 finger. The sum is 1 finger, 1 coil, 1 heel and 5 strokes, which is 10115. Check: 9608 + 507 = 10115.
(ii) Strokes: 6. Heels 8 + 4 = 12: 1 coil and 2 heels.
The sum is 1 lotus, 1 coil, 2 heels and 6 strokes, which is 1126. Check: 1080 + 46 = 1126.
items.answer: (i) 1 finger, 1 coil, 1 heel, 5 strokes, which is 10115 (ii) 1 lotus, 1 coil, 2 heels, 6 strokes, which is 1126

videos.answer: (i) 1 finger, 1 coil, 1 heel, 5 strokes, which is 10115 (ii) 1 lotus, 1 coil, 2 heels, 6 strokes, which is 1126

source: Figure it Out (adding with landmarks, question 2)

items.question: Add the following numerals that are in the base-5 system that we created: (1 circle, 2 hexagons, 1 square, 2 triangles) + (3 circles, 1 hexagon, 2 squares, 2 triangles). Remember that in this system, 5 times a landmark number gives the next one!
steps: Count each kind: circles 1 + 3 = 4, hexagons 2 + 1 = 3, squares 1 + 2 = 3, triangles 2 + 2 = 4.
No kind reaches 5, so nothing needs to be regrouped.
The sum is 4 circles, 3 hexagons, 3 squares and 4 triangles.
Check in our numerals: 182 + 412 = 594, and 500 + 75 + 15 + 4 = 594.
items.answer: 4 circles, 3 hexagons, 3 squares and 4 triangles, which is 594

videos.answer: 4 circles, 3 hexagons, 3 squares and 4 triangles, which is 594

source: Figure it Out (bases and their limits, question 3)

items.question: Give a simple rule to multiply a given number by 5 in the base-5 system that we created.
steps: Each landmark times 5 is the next landmark: 1 × 5 = 5, 5 × 5 = 25, 25 × 5 = 125.
By the distributive property, multiply every symbol of the number by 5.
So every triangle becomes a square, every square a hexagon, every hexagon a circle, and so on.
Rule: replace each symbol by the symbol of the next landmark.
items.answer: Replace every symbol by the symbol of the next landmark

videos.answer: Replace every symbol by the symbol of the next landmark

source: Group 4000 into powers of 60 and say how it is written in ba

items.question: Group 4000 into powers of 60 and say how it is written in base 60 with our own symbols.
steps: The landmarks are 1, 60 and 3600; 216000 is far too big.
It is written as 1 with the 3600 symbol, 6 with the 60 symbol, and 40.

source: Regroup (2) × 3600 + (75) × 60 + 10 so that no count is 60 o

items.question: Regroup (2) × 3600 + (75) × 60 + 10 so that no count is 60 or more.
steps: 75 sixties is 60 sixties and 15 sixties.
60 sixties make one 3600, so the 3600s go from 2 to 3.

source: Write 3725 in the Mesopotamian place value system, using our

items.question: Write 3725 in the Mesopotamian place value system, using our numerals for each place.
steps: Dropping the landmark symbols, it is written 1 | 2 | 5: 1 in the 3600s place, 2 in the 60s place, 5 in the 1s place.

source: Figure it Out (Mesopotamian numerals, question 1)

items.question: Represent the following numbers in the Mesopotamian system: (i) 63 (ii) 132 (iii) 200 (iv) 60 (v) 3605
steps: (iv) 60 = (1) × 60, so the 1s place is empty: written 1 followed by a blank.
(v) 3605 = (1) × 3600 + 5, so the 60s place is empty: written 1 | blank | 5.
items.answer: (i) 1 | 3 (ii) 2 | 12 (iii) 3 | 20 (iv) 1 | blank (v) 1 | blank | 5

videos.answer: (i) 1 | 3 (ii) 2 | 12 (iii) 3 | 20 (iv) 1 | blank (v) 1 | blank | 5

source: A Mesopotamian numeral shows 2 and then 5, with a gap betwee

items.question: A Mesopotamian numeral shows 2 and then 5, with a gap between them that might hide an empty place. What two numbers could it be?
steps: If there is no empty place, 2 counts 60s and 5 counts 1s: 2 × 60 + 5 = 125.
If an empty 60s place is hidden in the gap, 2 counts 3600s: 2 × 3600 + 5 = 7205.
The same marks give 125 or 7205.
A placeholder written in the empty place would remove the doubt.
items.answer: 125 or 7205; only a placeholder for the empty place settles it

items.question: A Mayan numeral shows, from top to bottom, two dots, then three dots, then one bar. What number is it?
steps: Read from the bottom: the lowest place counts 1s, the next 20s, the top 360s.
The bottom is one bar, which is 5. The middle is three dots, which is 3. The top is two dots, which is 2.
So the number is 2 × 360 + 3 × 20 + 5.

source: Write 77, 100, 361 and 721 in Mayan numerals.

items.question: Write 77, 100, 361 and 721 in Mayan numerals.
steps: 77 = 3 × 20 + 17: three dots over three bars and two dots.
100 = 5 × 20 + 0: one bar over a shell.
361 = 1 × 360 + 0 × 20 + 1: one dot, a shell, one dot, from top to bottom.
721 = 2 × 360 + 0 × 20 + 1: two dots, a shell, one dot.
items.answer: 77 is 3 | 17, 100 is 5 | shell, 361 is 1 | shell | 1, 721 is 2 | shell | 1

steps: Thousands: 5 in heng form. Hundreds: empty, so a blank. Tens: 7 in heng form. Units: 2 in zong form.
Reading back: 5 thousands, no hundreds, 7 tens, 2 units.
items.answer: 5 heng, a blank, 7 heng, 2 zong, which is 5072

items.question: Why do you think the Chinese alternated between the Zong and Heng symbols? If only the Zong symbols were to be used, how would 41 be represented? Could this numeral be interpreted in any other way if there is no significant space between two successive positions?
steps: Alternating shapes shows where one place ends and the next begins.
With zongs only, 41 is four vertical rods for the tens and one vertical rod for the units: 5 rods in a row.
Without a clear gap, 5 rods could be read as 5, as 2 then 3 (23), as 3 then 2 (32), or as 1, 2, 2 (122).
So alternating zong and heng keeps neighbouring places apart.
items.answer: To keep neighbouring places apart; with zongs only 41 is 4 rods and 1 rod, which could also be read as 5, 23, 32 or 122

items.question: Read 4072 as digits times powers of 10, and explain what the 0 does.
steps: Places from the right: 1s, 10s, 100s, 1000s.
The 0 says there are no hundreds; without it the digits 4, 7, 2 would read 472.

items.question: Use the rules for 0 to find 25 + 0, 25 × 0, 25 − 25 and 3 − 7. Why do we need 0 and the negative numbers for every answer to be a number?
steps: 0 plus any number is that number: 25 + 0 = 25.
0 times any number is 0: 25 × 0 = 0.
A number minus itself is 0: 25 − 25 = 0, so 0 must be a number for this answer to exist.
3 − 7 = −4, a negative number; with 0 and the negatives, every sum, difference and product of two numbers stays in the set.
items.answer: 25, 0, 0 and −4; without 0 and negative numbers some differences would have no answer

items.question: Write 19 in base 8, in base 5 and in base 2.
steps: Base 8: one 8 would leave 11, so two 8s fit: 19 = (2) × 8 + 3, written 23.
Base 5: 19 = (3) × 5 + 4, written 34.
items.answer: 19 is written 23 in base 8, 34 in base 5 and 10011 in base 2

items.question: Form a base-2 place value system using 'ukasar' and 'urapon' as the digits. Compare this system with that of the Gumulgal's.
steps: Base 2 needs two digits: let urapon be 0 and ukasar be 1. The places are 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
1 is ukasar; 2 is ukasar urapon; 3 is ukasar ukasar; 4 is ukasar urapon urapon.
6 = (1) × 4 + (1) × 2 + (0) × 1, so 6 is ukasar ukasar urapon.
The Gumulgal joined words by adding (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar for 6) and stopped at 6; in the base-2 system the position gives each word its value, so it never runs out.
items.answer: With urapon as 0 and ukasar as 1, for example 6 is ukasar ukasar urapon; the place value version never runs out, while the Gumulgal names add up words and stop at 6

items.question: Where in your daily lives, and in which professions, do the Hindu numerals, and 0, play an important role? How might our lives have been different if our number system and 0 hadn't been invented or conceived of?
steps: Daily life: prices and bills, phone numbers, dates and times, scores, money in a bank.
Professions: shopkeepers, accountants, engineers, doctors reading doses, computer programmers.
Computers store everything in base 2 with only the digits 0 and 1.
Without place value and 0, every large number would need new symbols and calculation would be slow, so science, trade and technology would have grown much more slowly.
items.answer: Open answer: money, time, phones, computing, accounting and science all depend on them; without them calculation would be slow and much of modern technology would be hard to build

items.question: The ancient Indians likely used base 10 for the Hindu number system because humans have 10 fingers. But what if we had only 8 fingers? How would we be writing numbers then? What would the Hindu numerals look like if we were using base 8 instead? Base 5? Try writing the base-10 Hindu numeral 25 as base-8 and base-5 Hindu numerals, respectively. Can you write it in base-2?
steps: With 8 fingers we would use base 8: digits 0 to 7 and places 1, 8, 64, ...
25 = (3) × 8 + 1, so in base 8 it is written 31.
25 = (1) × 25 + (0) × 5 + 0, so in base 5 it is written 100.
items.answer: 25 is written 31 in base 8, 100 in base 5 and 11001 in base 2
